title: The Myth of Absinthe
summary: Josh and Chuck explore absinthe: what it is (a high-proof spirit flavored with fennel, anise and wormwood), wormwood's long history as a medicinal plant, the myths about thujone causing hallucinations and seizures, the Pierre Ordinaire and Henriod sisters origin story, the Dubied and Pernod families, the phylloxera-driven rise of cheap absinthe, its role in French art and Bohemian culture, the Jean Lanfray murder case and temperance campaign that led to bans, its legalization, and how to prepare it with water, sugar and the louche. Ends with listener mail about a Simpsons reference to postmodern art.

segments.title: Opening banter and absinthe introduction
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about the green fairy nickname and absinthe in movies, then introduce absinthe as a spirit flavored with wormwood, fennel and anise, and note wormwood's long medicinal history.

segments.title: Myths about wormwood and thujone
segments.summary: The hosts discuss wormwood's historical uses, the Ebers Papyrus reference, and malort. They explain thujone and debunk the claim that absinthe causes hallucinations and seizures, noting trace amounts in historical and modern recipes.

segments.title: Origin story: Pierre Ordinaire and the Dubied family
segments.summary: The popular origin story of Dr. Pierre Ordinaire in Couvet, Switzerland, is covered, along with doubts about it, the Henriod sisters, Major Henri-Louis Dubied, and the Pernod family merger that led to the Pernod brand.

segments.title: Spread to France, the army and phylloxera
segments.summary: Absinthe spreads through French soldiers given it in North Africa against malaria. Phylloxera devastates French vineyards, making wine expensive and cheap absinthe popular with working-class drinkers.

segments.title: Absinthe advertising and artists
segments.summary: Absinthe ads in France used patriotic and sexy imagery and even hygiene claims. Absinthe was popular in Europe among Bohemian artists, who believed it changed perception. Works by Manet, Van Gogh and Picasso are mentioned, along with Baudelaire, Wilde and Toulouse-Lautrec.

segments.title: Temperance movement and the Lanfray murder case
segments.summary: The temperance movement and wine makers targeted absinthe. Jean Lanfray murdered his family in 1905, and psychiatrists blamed absinthe madness. Valentin Magnan's wormwood experiments on dogs and the invented absinthism syndrome gave the campaign scientific cover.

segments.title: Absinthe bans and modern legalization
segments.summary: Absinthe was banned in Switzerland in 1910, the US in 1912, and France in 1915, with the UK never banning it. Pernod made a substitute in 1920. The EU lifted bans in the late 1980s, France removed its law around 1988 region-wide, and the US allowed it in 2007 under thujone limits and labeling rules.

segments.title: How to prepare absinthe: louche, drip and sazerac
segments.summary: The hosts explain how to prepare absinthe with ice-cold water to create the louche, use of a absinthe fountain and sugar cube, the legend of the Pernod distillery fire and the Dubs River, the risks of the flaming sugar method, and rinsing a glass for a Sazerac.

segments.title: Listener mail: Simpsons postmodern reference
segments.summary: A listener points out a Simpsons episode, Homer the Moe, that parallels the postmodern art discussion from a previous episode. Hosts close with the sign-off and contact info.
